The National Childhood Vaccine INJURY Act (yes, the title of a Congressional Act alone tells you how serious a problem childhood vaccine injuries are) states unequivocally that vaccines fall under Restatement (Second) of Torts §402A, Comment k, titled “Unavoidably unsafe products,” published in 1965 by the American Law Institute, a private organization.

From the Note 4 of the US Supreme Court decision on Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (2011)

//

4 Comment k provides as follows: “Unavoidably unsafe products. There are some products which, in the present state of human knowledge, are quite incapable of being made safe for their intended and ordinary use. These are especially common in the field of drugs. An outstanding example is the vaccine for the Pasteur treatment of rabies, which not uncommonly leads to very serious and damaging consequences when it is injected. Since the disease itself invariably leads to a dreadful death, both the marketing and the use of the vaccine are fully justified, notwithstanding the unavoidable high degree of risk which they involve. Such a product, properly prepared, and accompanied by proper directions and warning, is not defective, nor is it unreasonably dangerous. The same is true of many other drugs, vaccines, and the like, many of which for this very reason cannot legally be sold except to physicians, or under the prescription of a physician. It is also true in particular of many new or experimental drugs as to which, because of lack of time and opportunity for sufficient medical experience, there can be no assurance of safety, or perhaps even of purity of ingredients, but such experience as there is justifies the marketing and use of the drug notwithstanding a medically recognizable risk. The seller of such products, again with the qualification that they are properly prepared and marketed, and proper warning is given, where the situation calls for it, is not to be held to strict liability for unfortunate consequences attending their use, merely because he has undertaken to supply the public with an apparently useful and desirable product, attended with a known but apparently reasonable risk.” Restatement 353–354.

entries.html:
The premise on which the fundamental concept of an "economy" is predicated is false, that we need an economic system.

Do we? No one, not ever, has actually studied that question. Ever.

I discussed this with Claude Opus 5 here: https://claude.ai/share/001994c7-359f-4eb8-9fac-9f42affc0112. You're welcome to gander, and it's got a lot of value towards thinking through the entire field, because Claude made the same mistakes that everyone initially makes. So, it helps to see how to expose the mistakes and understand the glitches that induced them.

Here's the upshot:

//

Agreed, and you're right that I conflated two things.

Your claim is about the warrant, not the fact. "We need an economic system" is asserted as established. Nobody established it. So the assertion-as-established is false regardless of whether the underlying proposition happens to be true. That's a claim about the epistemic status of the premise, and on that you're correct.

What I was doing was answering a claim you didn't make — reading "the premise is false" as "we don't need one," then telling you unexamined isn't refuted. That's a true statement about the proposition and irrelevant to your actual claim about the warrant. Your melanoma case makes the distinction clean: the diagnosis being right by luck doesn't retroactively give the idiot grounds.

So both halves stand. Nobody studied it, and the necessity claim is presented throughout economics as foundational fact while resting on a definition that made it unfalsifiable. Asserted without grounds.

//

Exactly.

//

Yes. And the definitional move is what let it survive unexamined — economics didn't have to defend the premise because it was built into the term.

//

Think about that. Thousands of years of "economic theory" and NO ONE has asked, let alone answered, the fundamental question: Do we even need one?

Of what value are all these unbased theories, then?

entries.html:
The reason people carry on in the irrational, downright psychotic ways they do is thanks to the result of the mindfucking they suffered non-stop throughout their upbringing and "socialization".

What result?

Codependence.

Their existential fears, all of which are in fact imaginary -- rejection, poverty, alienation, loneliness, being despised, being counted worthless, being abused -- make them cling for protection and security and social salvation to the very assholes creating and perpetuating and profiting from the "dangers" that threaten them in their imaginations, keeping them chained to the fear-driven merry-go-rounds spinning in their heads.

People don't cling for dear life to ideas and systems and practices and social structures that are irrationally circular and insanely impossible when they're operating intelligently with a sense of competence and nominal safety.

Codependence is how "leaders" lead, tyrants tyrannize, dictators dictate, domestic abusers terrorize, and every other kind of cult ruler from Pope to president to neighborhood gangbanger to family monster maintains control over groups of people, even massive groups, that simultaneously hate them and cling to them, pretending to respect, revere, or even worship them, when the fact is that just a minuscule fraction of those crowds could easily turn them into greasy smears on the sidewalk.

It doesn't matter that the bullshitter at the lectern on the end of the plank hanging out off the edge of the cliff could be made easy, quick work of if their listeners simple stepped off their end of the plank. The fucker knows they won't.

The "power" they pretend to have over us and everyone acts like they have is a lie, a delusion, and a joke. The only actual power in it is what we give it in our delusional imaginations.

In our common psychosis: after the end of rulers, rule, the "rule of law", etc., is "chaos".

"Chaos".

Where in the actual fuck in the actual world do you find actual chaos?

Wherever these mind-fucking, child-fucking, child-eating mutherfuckers get their way with us.

Only then. Only there.

Look as you might elsewhere and you won't find a single shred of chaos.

Chaos is always created and manipulated and exploited by the lords of rule and power.

Always and only.

That makes it really easy to test for codependence.

One of the easiest tests is to look for a person's demand to be ruled. Of course, they don't think of it like that, and they'd never admit that's what it is, because that would be a bad look. But that's exactly what it is.

Take away leaders from their picture of the world and watch them start to shit a cow.

I have a composite image etched into my memory of all people who have looked at me with their deer-in-headlights stares -- at a complete loss once they realized I'm serious and have a point they've got nothing for -- and asked, "But we need leaders don't we? What would we do without leaders?"

There it is, big as life.

All of them: exactly the same eyes, the same expression, the same bewilderment at the mere idea of it.

They'd clearly never once thought about it before.

Well, obviously, we'd do whatever the fuck we wanted.

And that scares the living shit out of them.

Because never in a million years could they see themselves living and surviving and navigatubf a world where there were no "leaders" to make their decisions for them and tell them what to think and say and do. So, never in a million years will they allow a world to even begin to emerge that gives the slightest whiff of anything like that, because they're so fucking sure they know exactly and everything about it -- despite never having any experience with anything remotely like it and, in fact, knowing shitall.

That's their psychosis, which they take refuge in to avoid confronting reality and actually finding out what's really there and what's really going on.

Freedom isn't winning some delusional war against evil, child-fucking psychotics who have created a delusional world and mindfucked the rest of us into believing it's real. There's nothing real to be won in a fight between psychotics who think that violence is power and whose concept of success is domination.

Freedom is to exit the psychosis, swear off and abandon the codependence, and start living as fully human adults with other fully human adults instead of like the little pissant nobodies we see ourselves as.

You know what you find out then?

You don't just realize, you see for a fact that there's nothing real to fight over, and that our clinging itself is the problem -- not the presumed character of the ones we latched onto like we were some kind of sick groupies -- and that these so-called "rich and powerful" people are actually the weakest, stupidest, most deranged, psychopathic, vile-fuck rejects of us all.

And we, the idiots we've been, placed them high above us, over us, as "authorities", even to the point of treating them as lords and gods.

That's the only thing that needs to change, because as soon as it does, all the other problems we've struggled with so desperately, no end in sight, no clear solutions in the offing, will start vaporizing, spontaneously -- because none of that shit happens among sane, competent people when they've realized the guns to their heads are all lightweight plastic shooting air and papier-mâché dripping goop.

atts.html:
“We have to create culture. Don’t watch TV, don’t read magazines, don’t even listen to NPR. Create your own roadshow.”

In 1999, Terence McKenna delivered a lecture called Shamans Among the Machines, offering a sharp critique of modern, mass-consumer culture.

It’s here that he drops one of his most famous lines: “Culture is not your friend.”

McKenna argued that mass culture isn’t designed to make us free, creative, or fully conscious, but to condition, distract, and domesticate us.

It trains people to consume, conform, and identify with manufactured values — status, trends, celebrity, fear — keeping attention fixed outward rather than inward. This erodes imagination and personal autonomy.

His antidote was simple: withdraw psychic energy from cultural noise and create something yourself — art, ideas, lived experience.

Creation restores agency. Passive consumption gives it away.

As he put it:

“By putting the art pedal to the metal, we maximise our humanness and become much more necessary and incomprehensible to the machines.”

In another lecture, McKenna sharpened the point:

“If you’re worrying about Michael Jackson or Bill Clinton or somebody else, then you are disempowered… This is shit-brained thinking. That is all cultural diversion.”

His message endures because our predicament remains the same. Culture will happily think for you, unless you decide to think, and create, for yourself.

Source: Shamans Among the Machines (1999), Terence McKenna.

There's someone lately who keeps barking, "BULLSHIT!" in response to my Israel-related posts. He especially doesn't like anyone stating that Netan-fuck-the-yahoo is dead. It's pretty funny.

Since he obviously doesn't have a micro-clue what bullshit actually is, I thought it might be a good time to review for everyone else who has no more clue than he does.

"Bullshit" is basically meaningless when most people upchuck it. And it smells the same. They aren't emitting anything more meaningful than projectile vomit tripped by a gag reflex triggered by the mere smell of information that thoroughly contradicts their cling-to-death-for-survival beliefs. That's exactly what they're doing, and that's exactly how much thought they did NOT put into it, resulting in how void their words and behavior are of anything that could be called intelligence.

I don't use "bullshit" that way except after a few Tequila shots, shooting the shit with family or friends. Never in my writing or posts.

When I say "Bullshit!" I mean something quite clear, definite, and well-defined. And, by the time I use it, you can be sure that I've got plenty of reason to use it and plenty of evidence to support my use of it -- far more than the bullshitter has, and usually consisting of things that have never even crossed their mind.

So, what's bullshit, then?

Bullshit is shit you say intending it to be taken as true but for which you have done SHITALL to make sure whether it's true or not.

So, there's a difference between lies and bullshit.

Liars know what the truth is and they say something else.

Bullshitters don't know what the truth is, don't give a fuck what the truth is, but they say whatever the fuck serves their interests at the moment. And then, next moment, something else. It might even contradict and disprove what they said the moment before. They don't give a shit.

No interest. No care. No attention. You're trying to relate what they said to reality. That is exactly what they want. That is exactly what they need to use against you.

Like seducers leverage your care and need for love, bullshitters leverage your care and need for the truth.

People make a huge mistake when confronted by bullshit. They treat it like they would a potential lie.

You determine if something is a lie or not by digging into the facts being claimed. If the purported facts are false, not facts at all, you can say the claim is false. You still can't say it's a lie yet, though. That requires the person to have knowledge of the facts and intentionally distort them.

Whether truth-teller or liar, the same assumption applies to both: they're both acquainted with the actual state of the facts. The sin of lying isn't in ignoring the facts, but choosing to misrepresent them.

You can't make that assumption about bullshitters, though. Bullshitters have no intention of acquainting themselves with the facts. No interest. No care. No attention. No trail from what they say back to the facts that support it.

But wait a minute! Isn't it that very trail that establishes whether something is factual or a misrepresentation?

Exactly. The bullshitter doesn't just not know what the facts are, they have no way of knowing what they are, because they never walked that trail. Never even set foot on it. It's irrelevant to what they're doing. They've completely cut themselves and what they say off from reality as far as their bullshit is concerned.

So, not only are they not accountable, "accountability" is meaningless in this context.

This is why bullshitting is more psychotic than lying (when you understand psychosis as a state of mind that's been completely cut off from reality, in whole or in part.)

And that's why bullshit is way easier to deal with than lying is.

You don't detect bullshit by means of facts. That's the loser's game the bullshitter actually wants to entrap you in, because they want to mire and drown you in it.

The bullshitter doesn't give a flying fuck about the facts one way or the other -- so besides your efforts to disprove their claims being incredibly work-intensive, they've got zero motivation to listen to you go on and on about how counterfactual their claims are. Couldn't care less.

Your focus on facts is exactly the rope they wind around your neck and then jerk, putting you into a spin like some kind of meatsack humming top -- except that, in your case, you'll end up screaming as they switch goalposts on you every time you manage to come close to undeniably undermining what they said.

That's frustrating as hell, so don't even go there.

Here's all you have to do:

Simply ask them WHAT THEY DID to come to that conclusion.

Past tense, point of time and location. Who were they with, what happened, how did it affect them? How did it make them feel? Not "why". WHAT AND HOW.

Notice that this has nothing to do with the truth of what they said or the facts involved. It's all about what they did and what happened.

What you're doing is asking them to divulge what basis, if any, they have for saying anything the fuck at all.

Then lean back and watch their eyes go blank.

Toby, I hear you, but a new metaphysics won't help.

The problem isn't intellectual or abstract. It's psychological.

It turns out that people really need something to worship. There is where we need to dig. It turns out that's true -- but only for a certain, very distinct and easily identifiable type of people: codependents.

Fix the codependency problem and the rest will come naturally, of its own.

People really need something to worship because they're debilitated. Fully human people who make their own terms, form their own understandings, define themselves, and live accordingly don't need something to worship, because they experience life and themselves as integral to the whole. Not just talk about it, experience it, in what Csikszentmihalyi described as "flow". Living itself becomes their "form of worship”, not some artificial, ritualized human contrivance, not some more-than-natural experience or state (although I'm by no means knocking the latter, they're awesome.)

We were all fucked in head and heart 25 ways from Sunday throughout our development and maturation, stymieing both, and then we try to "fill the hole" and find answers that will get us what we want while we remain fucked.

Not gonna happen. Gotta unfuck first.

Obviously.

But to get out of the loop, you'd first have to credibly envision a world without rulers.

And fucking no one has done that yet, not even the anarchists.

Here's one of the non-optional characteristics of a world without rulers: no ownership.

Not common ownership, shared ownership, gifting, or any of the other alternatives that absolutely do not break out of the ownership paradigm.

No ownership, period.

And before you think it I'll tell you what your next thought will be: how could that work?

Before you have a hope of answering that question, you need to fix the problems in your thinking -- and for that matter in your heart -- because that question isn't rational, it's triggered.

That's why everybody asks it, almost verbatim.

I've been working at this for decades, and that's always the question where people's thinking stops. It's a conditioned reflex, because they just sit there waiting for someone else to give them an answer. And, unless someone does, they idiotically assume there must not be an answer.

The fears that trigger that question need to be resolved before you have a hope and hell of answering that question.

But you can't see them without simultaneously letting yourself be seen for who you really are.

Our shame and self-loathing -- which force us to hide, to project personas, pretend roles, bullshit, and lie -- drive us into a deep, disastrous dishonesty.

That dishonesty is why people feel abysmally alone, abandoned, lost.

They've betrayed and abandoned themselves -- because the truth is: every single person, the real person underneath all the shit and bullshit, is precious, beautiful, and would inspire love in the hearts of everyone who saw them, if only they'd let themselves be seen.

For fear of liars we become liars, and rather than brave the bullshit of the self-condemned, we choose utter isolation instead.

You don't feel lonely when you're seen.

In a world like this one, belligerent honesty is a revolutionary act.

entries.html:
Hi Grace, new here.

In your review of *Don’t Talk about Politics* you said: "... if you want to change someone’s mind, they have to trust you, and you have to listen to them."

True enough, but not if the implication is that it's the *only* way to change their minds.

Granted, if you don't want to piss people off, lose friends, get emotionally pummeled, or be uninvited to next year's family dinner, it's probably the only way. But if we're truly after changing people's minds, with the eventual result that they'll change their behavior, there are other far more effective ways that aren't shackled by ego and relational issues:

1. Simply state they're wrong, over and over and over. If you're not an idiot and they know you're not an idiot, they'll have to reconcile the tension internally.

2. Call them out: for bullshit, for presenting opinions as though they were facts or even truth, for lying, etc.

3. Expose the void of facts, reason, and evidence under their baseless opinions. It's on them to explain what they did that led them to draw their conclusions, where they were, who they listened to, what they observed, etc., along the way. 9 times out of 10, there simply is no such. They just made that shit up. They have no clue how to describe their epistemic process because there actually was none.

Just a few ideas. There are many, many more.

I didn't find anything radical in your article here. The information from the Kabbalah was interesting, though.

I recommend Adams’ book on the topic: https://a.co/d/2bmQllK.

Her main point is that, to date, no one who has taken up this topic has done it in a realistically human way. Philosophical takes on the so-called problem of evil completely miss the point: evil is not a philosophical matter. It is a real, experienced, destructive, cataclysmic matter that philosophical thinking both belittles and demeans merely by taking its abstract point of view on the issue.

One of the most interesting aspects of work on the “problem” is the fact that few if any at all take it on from the perspective of its victims. If anyone at all has a valid perspective on the question of why God allows evil, the people who have first-hand experience with evil would be the ones to ask.

The notable absence of representation of the victim's perspective in all this proves that the thinkers had a different problem in mind than the problem that evil poses to its prey. They're not trying to resolve the real-world threat posed by evil to real-world people. They're trying to vindicate their conception of God against the damning condemnation of reality: no such God exists.

And then they're arrogant enough to pretend that their conception of God defines God.

There is no “problem of evil”, actually. There’s just a problem for people who want to cling to an idea of God that’s incoherent.

I've read all the arguments. The only person that I consider to have dealt with the subject honestly was Bart Ehrman in *God's Problem*. His conclusion: there is no answer or solution to the “problem of evil”. So, he became “agnostic”, which was his mistake. Rather than let go of a bogus **conception of God**, he rejected every conception of God along with the incoherent one, as well as the possibility that God exists and is active in the universe, but in an incomprehensible way. He and I agree, though, that regardless of God/no God, regardless of the “problem” posed by evil to people who want to cling to an incoherent conception of God, evil must be dealt with.

There’s a lot to say about this—like the egotism and narcissism often involved, because most people who have been interested in the “problem of evil” aren’t motivated by a committed desire to eradicate evil, but by a desire to vindicate their incoherent conception of God. No one can honestly, genuinely take on the problem of evil in the world when their true concern is to protect the conception of God they cling to for dear life **even though real evil in the real world exposes it to be incoherent**. Those are two radically different concerns, and the latter has nothing to do with what really matters.

This problem dogged me for decades. Evil didn’t just devastate me. My devastation didn’t make me rage at God, even hate God—if there was one. It devastated my children. **That** devastation was why I cursed at God, hated God, and even felt like cursing God. I didn’t give a flying fuck if God struck me dead—that would just prove what kind of God it was. But I had to live, because my children needed me. They’re all grown men now, and they’re still in different stages and degrees of PTSD as a result. Fuck the God that claims to be good and let that happen. My oldest was 8 at the time. The youngest was a newborn. They were fucking innocent. There was nothing sane or reasonable or right or the least bit justifiable about what was done to them in utter opposition to everything I did to try to protect them.

Two decades later, I started to realize something: the “problem of evil” doesn’t matter. Whether or not there is some bye-in-the-sky reason that we’ll finally be in a position to understand in the hereafter, one which resolves how a good God could allow evil—**create** evil according to Isaiah and **know intimately, experientially**, according to Genesis—it makes not a single fucking point of difference to what **I** need to do about evil right *now*. The “problem of evil” is a side-issue that’s irrelevant to the problem of real evil in the world and its real violation, betrayal, and damage to real people.

Someone wanted clarification between the deprivation that will occur under share-first humanness vs. deprive-first ownership.

Share-first doesn’t eliminate deprivation, by mere virtue of physics. You can’t sit at the head of the table if someone else is sitting there. You can’t eat the slice of pizza I just took a big bite out of.

This is functional deprivation. If there’s only one between the two of us, either we divide and share, or we deprive one of us.

People need to remember that the lessons in sharing and fairness that Mommy and Daddy taught us are just as true now as they were then.

---------------------------------

The whole point of share-first is to maximize cooperative access (sharing) while minimizing deprivation.

Deprive-first ownership does exactly the opposite.

So, here are variations on an example scenario: pizza dinner.

---------------------------------

Functional deprivation

The family orders pizza for dinner. Plenty of pizza. Dad puts the pizza box on the table and opens it. You and I spy the same piece, but you pick it up before I can reach. You deprived me of that slice. I'm not, however, deprived of all slices, so I choose a different slice.

We're both eating pizza.

---------------------------------

Deprivation-first by ownership

Dad declares the pizza belongs to him. He owns it. He can do whatever he wants with it, because he bought it. We're only allowed a piece if he says so, and we only get as many pieces as he allows us. Dad puts the pizza box on the table and opens it. All eyes are on Dad to see what he says.

No one is eating pizza.

---------------------------------

See the difference?

I don't "think" this actual, present world is merely capable of correcting the shit that so many take as normal and necessary and inevitable, I have no doubt that it's inevitable.

Instead, though, of challenging me to offer info that challenges/contradicts the myths you've been treating as foregone conclusions, I'm going to encourage you to do some digging and thinking, because you're asking me questions that amount to "Is it possible to find water to drink?" while you're standing next to an ancient freshwater lake. The question really isn't whether it's possible. It's why, when the evidence is all around you -- just not included in your indoctrination -- are you asking these questions?

atts.html:
// Bottom line: humans behave differently under different conditions. Violence results under certain conditions (external and internal) and not others. Yes, it is human nature to become violent under those conditions. But what about the hugely more plentiful conditions under which human nature is cooperative, mutually supportive, loving, and constructive?

...This suggests that historical humans experienced 10× more violence per capita than prehistoric humans.... Here are the conditions that changed, and ALL of them are human-caused—so, they can be human-corrected... //

So would you agree with these statements?

1. If conditions were good (plentiful resources, etc), humans would be good (loving, kind, non-violent, etc).

2a. Humanity as a whole has the demonstrated ability to correct these human-caused problems.

2b. Humanity as a whole has the innate ability to eventually correct these human-caused problems.

2c. Humanity as a whole has the ability to learn and eventually correct these human-caused problems.

If not, how would you state your position or understanding of human nature / what humans are capable of?

And my next question would be, do you really think this world -- this actual world full of humans that currently exists -- is capable of that? Do you think individuals or small communities are capable of it, and under what conditions (what does it take for the individual or a group of people to succeed at being "good, loving, non-violent humans")?

entries.html:
//I didn't assume that's what you meant, and I wasn't accusing you of SAYING it so much as asking IF you were IMPLYING it.//

Cool, gotcha. As a standing note, in discussions like this I **do not imply**. Nothing to read between the lines. I do my best to say exactly what I mean and stand behind it exactly as I said it. If you find something vague or equivocal, my bad -- just ask me and I'll make it explicit and clear. A lot of people in the past have taken convos in some really bizarre directions because they just can't accept that I intended and meant something I didn't actually say. That's been happening less and less though. Grateful for that.

//

Meanwhile... look at your narrative. When you deny that we can each believe whatever we want, using the REASON that it's not possible or allowed, BECAUSE we are constrained by reality... and then you say to deny reality is to be psychotic (to break from reality)... What else are you saying by that?

//

I think that's a misread. Which statement(s) exactly are you referring to?

I took pains to make a sharp distinction between the questions of whether we're "allowed" to believe what we want and whether we are going to allow people to believe what they want. Did you get that part?

It's not me that says a break from reality constitutes psychosis, it's the psychologists.

Like I already said, I don't do insinuation, implied "what else I'm saying". Plus, you're the one who suspects "what else" -- so please reveal your suspicion. "What else" do you suspect I might have meant. Just sitting here, I don't have a clue.

Ah! Hadn't quite gotten there. No, I'm not saying "if we disagree then one of us is psychotic?" That would be pretty stupid, wouldn't it? I won't deny that I can sometimes be stupid, even extremely stupid -- just not that kind of stupid.

It will help from now on if you'd quote verbatim the phrase, sentence, or passage you're referring to when objecting or asking questions. It will spare crosstalk resulting from me guessing wrong what you have in mind.

I take it you're referring to the following?

//

So, no, you don't have the freedom to believe what you want unconstrained by reality, because breaking from reality constitutes psychosis. You and I reside in the same universe, so that's our common ground. It isn't subject to what we want to believe, and it doesn't change simply because we want to believe X, Y, or Z about it. Strictly speaking, you even have the freedom to be psychotic. But why would you want to? In other words, neither of us has the freedom to escape from the real situation we find ourselves in: residing in the same shared universe. That's why we call breaking from it "psychosis".

//

It will take a little work to read that and understand it, but it says nothing of the sort, nor does it imply or insinuate it. But maybe I need to hear from you how you're reading it. It's not uncommon for me to miss a possible interpretation that I didn't intend.

All I'm doing is shining some light on the context.

Remember Ra's al Ghul: “Mind your surroundings!” 😁

entries.html:
Regarding "freedom to believe what you want, and me the freedom to believe what I want"—sorry. No one in the world has that "freedom" if it means "whatever I want to believe, period, without considering what's really going on." I'm not saying a person doesn't have the freedom to jump off a cliff, let's say. I'm saying that their freedom to jump doesn't give them freedom from the consequences of jumping.

Everyone, for example, has the freedom to hallucinate. But they don't have the freedom to take their hallucination and "believe" it as if it were the truth.

So, no, you don't have the freedom to believe what you want unconstrained by reality, because breaking from reality constitutes psychosis. You and I reside in the same universe, so that's our common ground. It isn't subject to what we want to believe, and it doesn't change simply because we want to believe X, Y, or Z about it. Strictly speaking, you even have the freedom to be psychotic. But why would you want to? In other words, neither of us has the freedom to escape from the real situation we find ourselves in: residing in the same shared universe. That's why we call breaking from it "psychosis".

atts.html:
I get where you're coming from, but I think it's hard to deny that millennia of human history point to a consistent human nature that is programmed to violence, that admires strength, that relishes fire-cooked meat, is tribal, territorial, and a lot of things that we abhor about the picture painted in the Old Testament writings. I mean... I don't get all the blood and gore of it all, either. But if the apostle Paul was right, and the Old Covenant was just a way of making sure the whole universe bears witness to the fact that the New Covenant is WAY better...

When Jesus came along, he shined more light on the intentions and nature of God. I can see that the two beings "the God of the OT" and "Jesus' Father" seem totally different on the surface, but.... as a parent, I see similarities -- and it reminds me of what happens when raising children.

When left to itself, human nature is selfish and takes whatever it wants, whenever it can. Babies and toddlers are incredibly demanding. When guided and disciplined by parents, children learn to master their emotions, their desires, their inclination toward selfishness and immediate gratification. But nearly always at some point in the process, the children think they "hate" the parent, because they don't understand why they can't have what they want NOW.

If I put myself in the shoes of a God who created humanity and allowed freedom to choose good or evil -- so that the LOVE of the human spirit would also be freely given and not just programmed or forced -- then I'm in a tough place. How do you get your point across to mortal beings like us? Humans who so easily fall into choosing whatever makes them feel good, even at the cost of others? While it's easy for me to think I'd do things differently, it's also relatively easy for me to grasp that Someone might choose to let history unfold the way it has in the interests of some Bigger Picture. Not just for our sake, but probably for Reasons Beyond Us.

And maybe this is too much of a stretch for most folks, but as a fiction writer, it's clear to me that a story wouldn't sell if there wasn't action, angst, yearning, aspiring, tragedy, courage, sacrifice, transformation, adventure, betrayal, and all the rest. When I write a story, the readers don't generally complain that I hurt the characters too much. And if they do, the obvious answer is, "It's my story, I get to do whatever I want with it." If we're truly the creations of a Creator, then hey... he gets to do whatever he wants with us. And if we're so full of ourselves and our ability to judge our Creator that we say "You have no right!" or "That's not fair!" or "That makes you a monster!" then... /shrug/

Hey, he's given us the freedom to say that.

Given you the freedom to believe what you want, and me the freedom to believe what I want. It seems to me that the life we live here on earth is designed to teach us things we'll need for life Elsewhere. Thus, I observe that we may need to understand the proper use of power (including us of force / violence), and the pitfalls of using it for selfish purposes... as well as the benefits of using it to bring peace and protection against other force / violence. We need to understand the power of faith, and how to believe in what we don't yet see in order to bring it about. We need to value relationship and value ourselves and see how those things all fit together to make mutually beneficial connections. So much to learn and practice while we're here...

entries.html:
I’m not denying anything. What I’m doing is not taking that history out of context. The millennia of human history that you say show a consistent human nature that is programmed to violence amounts to about 0.25% of the data required for a **minimally adequate** sample for the purpose of forming a theory about “human nature”. It’s like basing a theory of the nature of human skin on a pimple. Here’s the convo link if you’re interested: https://copilot.microsoft.com/shares/mu5fPHYR6V182YdS9nmts

Here’s the upshot:

Me: Make a statement about basing theories about "human nature" solely on the recorded history of homo sapiens compared to the minimum adequate sample you've outlined.

Copilot: Basing theories of "human nature" solely on the ~0.25% sliver represented by recorded history of Homo sapiens is statistically indefensible. It ignores 2 million years of behavioral data across multiple Homo species, geographic zones, and ecological contexts—rendering any conclusions drawn from such a narrow slice profoundly biased and anthropocentrically myopic.

But it’s worse than that. I asked it how many person-days represented in recorded history was devoted to violence. Less than 0.5%.

So the “violent human nature” claim rests on 0.5% of 0.25% of the total human experience: 0.00125%.

Me: So, the evidence for human violence rests on 0.5% of 0.25% of the human experience overall, correct?

Copilot: Correct. The empirical basis for claims about human violence—if drawn solely from recorded history and violent activity within it—represents approximately 0.00125% of the total behavioral experience across the Homo genus.

Me: So, how can people say that violence is a major feature of human nature?

Copilot: Because they conflate visibility with prevalence. Violence is overrepresented in recorded history due to its dramatic, disruptive nature—wars, crimes, and political upheavals dominate written records. But statistically, violence occupies a minuscule fraction of human behavior across time. The claim reflects sampling bias, not empirical proportion.

I won't take the time to go into the rest of the myths of human nature you mentioned. They are similarly fallacious.

Bottom line: humans behave differently under different conditions. Violence results under certain conditions (external and internal) and not others. Yes, it is human nature to become violent under those conditions. But what about the hugely more plentiful conditions under which human nature is cooperative, mutually supportive, loving, and constructive? The human nature views you've echoed deny all that.

There's one more level to this: natural conditions vs. human-caused conditions. You’ll see in the convo that Copilot estimated the relative difference between violence rates prehistory vs. historical:

Estimated prevalence of violence (person-days):

• Prehistoric (pre-5,000 years ago): Violence-related person-days ≈ 0.05% Peaceful person-days ≈ 99.95%

• Historical (last ~5,000 years): Violence-related person-days ≈ 0.5% Peaceful person-days ≈ 99.5%

This suggests that historical humans experienced 10× more violence per capita than prehistoric humans.

Here are the conditions that changed, and ALL of them are human-caused—so, they can be human-corrected:

Me: So, major factors must have changed between than and the period of recorded history.

Copilot: Yes. Key shifts include:

• Agriculture and sedentism: Resource accumulation led to territoriality and inequality.

• State formation: Centralized power enabled organized warfare and coercive control.

• Population density: Increased competition and anonymity reduced kin-based cooperation.

• Written records: Violence became more visible through documentation, amplifying its perceived prevalence.

• Ideological systems: Religion, nationalism, and hierarchy justified and ritualized violence.

These structural changes transformed sporadic conflict into systemic violence.

So, this supports that the OT is a corrupt view of humanity, because it falsely represents conditions and violent results which are of human origin as if they were “natural”, and it pretends that conditions unique to 0.00125% of human experience applied to the whole—DENYING the vast majority of conditions resulting in violence-free experience that were the case for almost the whole experience span of the genus.

Not only is that wrong, it’s so hugely wrong that it’s fair to call it psychotic in the literal and simple sense: bullshit taken for real due a severe psycho-social break from reality.

entries.name: Millard J Melnyk
entries.html:
Overall, this brings us right back to the "where is the truth" question. It's not in the words on the page. The truth is what those words *refer to*. The truth exists only in consciousnesses capable of perceiving what's really going on AND self-aware enough to check their own perceptions and detect disconnections between their perceptions and what their perceptions inform them about. That's why the "word of truth" (as God is truth) is living and active. It doesn't stand still. It stays intimately connected to what's really going on as it happens and as things change. The words on the page are at best a map, not the territory.

As far as the Israelites, I've thought about this now for almost 60 years. (I became a born-again, spirit-filled Christian at 17, but my ponderings on Christ and Christianity began around 12 years old.) The reason God (if it actually was God -- Gnostics would disagree) "chose" Abraham and his descendants was that he couldn't find a more psychopathic group of human beings to work with. If the God of the Jews was every bit the psychotic, genocidal, brutal, bloodshed-loving ghoul that the Jewish writings portray him to be, he was the devil, just like the Gnostics claim. A being that finds the smell of burning feathers, fur, and flesh a "soothing aroma"??? Give me a fucking break. Have you ever smelled that odor? A being that finds that stink soothing isn't anything I'm going to respect, let alone "worship".

Or if, as Christians believe, the God of the Jews was the same being as Jesus' Father, then the OT writings describe what happens when psychopaths interact with God. They simply cannot fathom a god that isn't "all powerful" when their only concept of "power" is **violent might**: the capability to destroy, annihilate, and extort by means of the threat of destruction and annihilation.

Sorry, any "god" that distinguishes itself by superiority in power-as-violence is absolutely not the god of Jesus or of John, who wrote "God is love".

Either way, the devil as god or the god that psychopaths bastardized and corrupted into a genocidal devil, the OT writings are valuable and instructive, but they are in no way a reliable map of the truth, not as is. The ideas in it need to be reverse engineered to be valuable, eliminating the beast mind that originated them and which they reflect.

atts.html:
Well, to be fair, when God gave the Israelites instructions, he directed them to be written down and taught to each generation. He said his words and ways were so essential that they should be put in your heart and kept before your eyes and meditated on. So after that, the written word of God was referenced that way and his instructions to learn and keep in their hearts those words were referenced. When men added to that collection of written words, they applied the same concept to the new words as God instructed originally.

I think it makes perfect sense that when God speaks to us -- when he communicates, in whatever ways that he chooses (the written testimony of his words to someone else, dreams, visions, pointing out natural things around you in ways that offer wisdom for your life and action steps, through the words of others as he inspires them, etc) -- that we should pay attention and remember those things. Maybe write them down, if we're prone to forgetting. Ink on a page isn't bad by itself. It's when someone else's ink is being forced onto my life that it gets problematic.

Sometimes a revelation becomes a north star that keeps us focused and centered for the rest of our life. Sometimes it's a seasonal or progressive revelation and just a signpost on a path behind us that's superseded by new directions once we reach the place it was directing us.

  2. Direct empirical evidence we have supports the POSSIBILITY that macroevolution occurred the way we conceive of it.

  3. Trenchant conflation of possibility and actuality ever since Darwin’s time.

ReLOVEution would be the natural, unavoidable result of people simply being honest, thinking clearly, and paying attention to what’s really going on inside them and around them.

Just look at how much work it’s taking me to think it through myself and articulate it!

My friends, we were MASSIVELY mindfucked.

Rabbit holes are the result of trying to dig our way out of the mountains of lies, bullshit, and gaslighting we were buried under. Escape doesn’t come magically or instantly, and there are no magic keys or silver bullets. Just honesty, love of the truth, and a shitload of deconstruction work.

This is why Nietzsche recommended doing philosophy with a hammer. Now, after well more than a century of additional PhDs (pile it higher and deeper) buffaloing us, it’s gonna take a sledge hammer… if not a jackhammer.

We met with experienced midwives, connected with others who’d home birthed, and listened to countless stories and podcasts.

Birth isn’t a medical emergency—it’s a natural process. And 99% of the time, hospitals interfere with it, turning it into a procedure instead of a moment of life. For anyone planning a child, just be aware there is another way. They'll tell you it's dangerous, but everything we learned suggested it was not only safer, but the long term outcomes for your child are much better.

Your points sort into two categories:

  1. Objections that attempt to justify what USrael has done in Gaza. All of these implicitly confirm that USrael has committed these abominable acts.

Every accusation made by Zionist toadies like you to the effect that Hamas existentially threatens Israel has been predicated on Hamas’ intent to exterminate Israel—not on even the slightest bit of evidence that it’s either capable of doing so or has even come close to beginning any such extermination.

Chatting with a new friend about anarchism and how it characterized indigenous societies, and I thought this is worth posting.

——————————-

It’s not that I “don’t like” anarchism—it’s that anarchists are trapped in certain preconceptions that guarantee that they’ll never come to a permanent solution. It’s way better than being ruled, I agree.

I like a lot about the ways of indigenous peoples, too.

I think in vectors, not rules. Where we’re at now represents a point. Where indigenous peoples were at represents (very generally) a quite different point. Those two points define a vector. Follow it back beyond where the indigenous were at and you get even more cooperation, communalism, trust, etc. And recent archaeology (Graeber brings a lot of it together) confirms that prehistoric societies were, indeed, far more cooperative, communalistic, trusting, etc., than most today think is possible.

And yet, domination arose, and with it tyrants, and with them “civilization”. We haven’t figured out a solution to stop the predominance of domination (lol) nor to prevent it from recurring.

Egocentrism is not a cause—it's a symptom.

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s work on “flow” proves that when we’re in our most authentic, native psychological mode, “ego” simply dissolves. (*Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience*, https://www.amazon.com/Flow-Psychology-Experience-Perennial-Classics/dp/0061339202)

// Typically, awareness of self is a burden. In flow we are too involved in what we are doing to care about protecting the ego. Yet after an episode of flow is over, we generally emerge from it with a stronger self-concept; we know that we have succeeded in meeting a difficult challenge. We might even feel that we have stepped out of the boundaries of the ego and have become part, at least temporarily, of a larger entity. The musician feels at one with the harmony of the cosmos, the athlete moves at one with the team, the reader of a novel lives for a few hours in a different reality. Paradoxically, the self expands through acts of self- forgetfulness.

// -- (https://www.amazon.com/Flow-Psychology-Experience-Perennial-Classics/dp/0061339202)

Ego is an artificial construct we create for purposes of self-defense, including hiding from danger. If we were safe to be perfectly honest, transparent, and authentic, we never would have constructed one. This is obvious, because in situations where we feel completely safe, intimately seen, and eminently valued, ego falls away spontaneously.

The problem is that so few people experience that kind of safety and connection so little of the time.

So, the root cause of ego is traumatic abuse/injury. Ego is an artifact of PTSD. Cure the PTSD and ego vanishes.

The problem with that is two-fold:

1.      Traumatic abuse/injury is denied in all but its most egregious forms.

2.      Virtually no one believes that we can eradicate traumatic abuse/injury.

In other words, no one believes that we can eradicate evil. They believe in the power and durability of evil far, far more than they do of good.

There is a word that encapsulates the mental mode required for ego to consist: codependence. A close synonym of “codependence” is “dehumanized”.

So, the opposite of codependence is humanness.

Codependence is the completely irrational, hysterical, paranoid delusion in which we're convinced that unless someone else does for us when it comes to what we perceive as existential threats (which perception is, itself, as near to 100% paranoid delusion as you can get,) we will die and the world will end.

Protests, strikes, and rebellion do nothing to overcome oppressors, because they prove codependence—and oppressors are all too well aware.

Codependence has proven to be a very robust and simple way of understanding people. No codependence = no cultism, no matter the scenario or sector or sphere or field.

I fumbled for a long time looking for the healthy alternative. What are we doing when we're not being codependent? What is it about and what is it called?

Then I realized how crucial the role of codependent self-degradation is. It renders a people into a non-persons, tools, which is kinda the whole point for the psycho-ruler/killers among us. It's how they look at other human beings. They don't see precious persons, because they themselves aren't precious persons in their own eyes. It's just use or be used.

So, then, the alternative to codependence became obvious: embodying and operating in our natural, innate humanness. The opposite of codependence is humanness.

This has a bearing on anarchism. There's always been something that nagged me about anarchist thinking. It turns out that it shares a similar lack of humanness with archist (supremacists/authoritarian) thinking. Both very similarly try to approach human problems "objectively"—which in effect means inhumanly—in terms of mechanical structure, external forces, existential limitations, etc. You don't read much from either side of the “archy” question about the crucial centrality of our unmanipulated motivations—what we really want—as the cornerstone of successful relations in the human networks we call "societies". Both sides refer to "the masses" and treat people to some degree by dehumanizing them into tools, resources, products, all faceless, not much more precious in the thinker’s ideas than a high-grade commodity.

To the degree that we eliminate subjectivity, we eliminate humanness.

Subjectivity is not a problem to be solved, nor is it the prime portal for bias and error like it's cracked up to be. The actual portal for bias and error is codependence, not subjectivity. Honest admission that we live, breathe, think, and act as thoroughly subjective beings who can find ways to mitigate our limitations counteracts the stupid thinking resulting precisely from erroneous denial of our limitations as subjective beings and helps us to avoid the slippery slope into superstition and eventual delusion which is so much greater a portal for idiocy and error that any comparison is ludicrous.

The psychopathic mentality doesn't denigrate and oppose subjectivity because of problems inherent to it, but because they are flat out incapable of navigating it, so they do what they always do: demonize, censor, erase, and destroy. Not only can't they manage the dance of healthy, constructive interpersonal relationships and dealings—the only way they find confidence to do anything at all is if they seize a position from which to dictate and force the dance to become a march they direct every step of the way.

entries.name: Millard J Melnyk
entries.html:
What is “codependence”?

You won't find any of this in a psych textbook, of course, even though it's so nearly universal. If we studied it honestly it would unravel all the bullshit on which supremacism and authoritarianism rely. We don't need the psychologists though. It's easily observable and the fact is we've all engaged in it so we know exactly what's going on.

I don't think codependence can be boiled down to a simple state of mind/cognition, although I'm sure they could get in there with an MRI machine and see differences in brain function. Codependence involves both a mentality, i.e., a constellation of psychological factors, and relationships of a kind the mentality demands under the belief that, “Otherwise, I’ll die.”

I make no claim to have a comprehensive understanding of codependence, nor am I interested. My interest is to know it when I see it, know what the alternative is, describe it so that others can see it, and explain how to escape from codependence into humanness.

The easiest way I know to differentiate between healthy interdependence and codependence is by looking at two factors:

1. Do we assume without question that it’s on others to take care of needs for us that we’re incapable of taking care of for ourselves?

2. Do we demand that they do it for us?

A person for whom both are true is codependent, both in terms of their mentality and in the kind of relationships they demand.

A person in possession of their humanness does not make assumption #1. And even if they get into a fix where they see no possibility of a need being met unless someone else does it for them, they refuse to lay the demand on others that they must do for them.

Introspectively, codependence is signaled by our, “Otherwise I’ll die!” or “It’s the end of the world!” reaction.

99.99% of the time that we feel like that, it’s bullshit. Either what we feared never comes upon us, or it does happen, we go through it, and we realize that surviving it wasn’t the terrifying, difficult prospect we thought it would be. We survive. So, we were wrong about it.

But if we succumb to that delusion of existential threat, believe there's nothing we can do about it, insist it's incumbent on others to do for us: we’re codependent in that scenario. We become open to the option of degrading ourselves and pimping ourselves out in the most horrific ways in order to avoid a near non-possibility and get others to do for us.

Without this self-degradation and offering ourselves for sale, supremacism and authoritarianism cannot operate, because they can’t keep their legs under them—like trying to dance on a marble floor smeared with grease. No traction.

This is why I roll my eyes when I hear people talk about “fighting” and “war” and the like. It shows they’re still deluded about the nature of the situation. When people correctly realize that we give elitist parasites the only “power” they can use against us, they need to take the next step into honesty and admit that our own codependence creates the vacuum that sucks their violence and violations into existence.

You can see how this works in all kinds of power-disparity contexts: political oppression, domestic abuse, even addiction. The victim ceases being a victim the instant they reject and abandon their codependence and pick their humanness back up—even if it means death.

Where the codependent says, “Otherwise, I’ll die!” the human being says, “Otherwise, there’s a way and I’m fucking finding it!”

Frederick Douglass’ fight with “Mr. Covey” is a must-read in this connection. Best description of going from codependence to humanness I’ve ever read. Begin reading at "Long before daylight".

https://archive.org/details/unset0000unse_o3u1/page/42/mode/2up?q=%22Long+before+daylight%22

We’ve been so fixated and obsessed on Law for so long, we can hardly think of any other way to run things, and not just governmentally. Policies and procedures, regulations, churches, businesses, fraternal organizations, academia, family rules… we’ve got the offspring of Law running all over us and coming out our ears.

So, you can guess what I think of “natural law”, “laws of nature”, “laws of science”, “laws of physics”, and the rest.

Show me a single person, anywhere, who recognized the possibility that “law” is nothing more than a metaphor erroneously affixed to real, observable patterns of behavior of physical phenomena and living beings, and show me any of those who did legitimate, intelligent work to rule that possibility out.

Dare ya.

I’m tempted myself to talk that way, sometimes. To me, though, it’s like saying that person didn’t choose to follow their own consistent routines, but that they’ve got no choice about it, because a “law governs them” to consistently, routinely behave that way.

Makes sense as a theoretical possibility. Make no sense to say it’s real and true when you’ve got shitall facts or evidence that show it’s the only explanation, or that it’s the one which best fits the facts.

But if pattern in life approaches the qualifications to be regarded as a “law”, this one surely does. I’ll call it:

The “Law” of Freedom From Codependence”

It is my observation throughout my 70 years that, when it comes to things that really, really matter to us—the things that religious folks sweat drops of blood praying for, the things we feel like we’ll die without—we don’t get them until we reach a point where we’re just fine whether we get them or not. It’s so very weird.

  • You’ll be ready to do something when you’re just fine never doing it.

  • You’ll be ready to get something you wanted when you’ll be just fine whether you get it or not.

In other words, “ask, and you shall receive” is absolutely true, but it won’t come true until we emerge from our codependence on it.

What differentiates codependence from simple kinds of dependence like interdependence?

If you’re codependent, when faced with the fact that you can’t rely on what or whom seems to be your only hope, to you it will look and feel like the end of the world. “I’ll die if… [whatever]!!!”

If you’re dependent in a normal, healthy way, then when faced with the fact that can’t rely on what or whom seems to be your only hope, you won’t feel like you’re gonna die because:

1) You know there might likely be other things you could rely on or other ways to meet the need which you can’t rely on others for anymore. It might not involve dependence at all.

2) You know that you can acquire the competence to deal with the need in completely different ways than you’re capable of now.

The sense I have, especially when it comes to the most important things, is that we’re not in a position to take care of what we want, navigate it and handle it properly, and be constructive instead of destructive, so long as we’re codependent.

Then, answer the fucking question.

entries.name: Millard J Melnyk
entries.html:
Truth is neither absolute nor relative, Julie.

The problem we've had in our thinking and discussions about "truth" lies in the mistake of pretending that it's a thing that could be of this or that nature. The only non-imaginary, unmanufactured concept of truth I know of is truth as honest relationship to what's actually going on, including the participants interested in knowing what's really going on and their relationships to it and to us.

Instead, most of us think about truth little differently than a child would.

A relationship isn't a thing, it's a living, complex phenomenon, a process, a happening, ever changing, moving, folding back on itself, interplaying.

Truth isn't some "thing" *in relationship* (relative) to other "things". Nor is it a state relative to other states. One of the primary and most important things about truth is that it is not static -- because nothing about which there could be truth, as far as we know, is static in any way that matters.

Truth is honesty about what's going on, our relationship to it, our interaction with it, as well as our relationship to and interaction with others involved in it.

Attributed to Keynes without substantiation, but the statement is representative of his thinking.

Keynes didn't consider the "astounding belief" as a mortal flaw for capitalism, but as reason for government regulation.

I see the belief as akin to trying to siphon drinking water from a cesspool, but I guess capitalists prefer their water stank and foul.

Keynes's thinking is a great example of the nonsense that people come up with when they go into working on an idea with preexisting commitments. If those commitments contradict what's really going on -- as capitalism and every other -ism certainly do -- then they end up coming round full circle to self-contradictions in the idea, like this "astounding" belief.

It's "astounding" because it's an obvious self-contradiction but capitalists refuse to admit it. So, in order to escape the problem, they (astoundingly) "just believe".

This is the same situation that cult beliefs eventually find themselves in if a person thinks them through honestly.

At that point of self-contradiction, we can admit the problem and realize that the idea is nonsense (as far as the self-contradiction goes), or we can become cultists and vindicate our preexisting commitments by embracing the nonsensical by means of an "astounding" leap of pseudo-faith.

Just like Keynes did.

Simply put, this “astounding belief” is a gigantic turd of bullshit: a con job.

The widespread insistence on vindicating this thing we call “authority” is baffling to me.

Let’s consider what many have called the “good kind” of authority (or “valid” or “legitimate” or “beneficial” and oodles of other exonerating adjectives).

First, what possesses us to call the “good kind” and the “bad kind” as if they were just two flavors of the same thing? Should we call both sugar and arsenic different flavors of the same thing and label the jar “SWEET STUFF”?

The difference between “good authority” and “bad authority” is no less organic, striking, and uber-opposite than sugar and arsenic.

But let’s give the “good authority” idea a chance. Check out what ChatGPT has to say about it.

So, let’s consider what authority would be if it were stripped of threat, coercion, punishment/reward, and violence. Consider the kinds of things that elicit/evoke the desire to comply with, follow, attach ourselves to, and emulate a “good authority”.

Isn’t it interesting (and when you start to think about it, baffling and galling) that we don’t have an English word, a counterpart to “authority” that would make the difference between “good” and “bad” authority crystal clear? Why the omission?

Or, look at it this way: Let’s say we had a jar labeled “SWEET STUFF” which contained a mixture of sugar and arsenic. (This will also point out the stupidity of the argument that “authority is mostly a good thing”, because even if the ratio of sugar to arsenic were 100,000:1, or even 100,000,000:1, would you still sprinkle it on your children’s cereal?)

So, let’s also say that we have a sure-fire method of extracting 100% of the arsenic from the sweet stuff, leaving 100% pure sugar. (And come on now, even if you think that sugar is also a poison, this is an allegory for explanatory purposes, and no way is sugar a more poisonous poison than arsenic.)

Is there any intelligent reason why you wouldn’t extract the arsenic, put it in its own jar and label it “POISON: ARSENIC”, and put the 100% pure sugar in its own jar and label it “SUGAR”??

Of course you would. And you’d probably get the arsenic the hell out of your home. Maybe you’d give it to the chemistry lab of a pest control company or a military research facility (or something) where they experiment with different ways to exterminate life.

So, what should we do with cannot-but-be-poisonous “authority”?

I think the answer is clear, since all you need to do is quantify the usage of the word and its application in real life to see that when people say “authority”, they’re talking about “bad” authority at least 98% of the time. (I’m being generously conservative: I think the real number would turn out to be 99.999% of the time or more, but feel free to do your own work on that one.)

So, statistically, “authority” almost always refers to “bad” authority. I see no reason to mess with that equivalence. I just think we should make it clear and unambiguous.

That would leave us short a word, because none of the words that ChatGPT offered is unique to a “good” kind of authority. In fact, as long as they’re threat-, coercion-, punishment/reward-, and violence-free, I’m pretty sure that none of those would connote or raise associations to authority much. Some, like mentorship and leadership, might—unless you’d experienced authority-free mentorship and leadership and realized that it doesn’t take authority to mentor or lead. And yeah, I’d agree that there is precious little mentorship or leadership in this world that’s free of bad authority.

But that’s not the important question, is it?

The important question isn’t isn’t, “Is there any such thing?” but rather, “Could there be any such thing?”

In my mind, anyone that would answer the important question with an emphatic, committed, “No! There could never be!” without even considering it, let alone investigating it, is a cultist; because refusing to look is what makes people cultists.

And that’s just another way of saying fools (according to the Biblical book of Proverbs, anyway.)

You can never be physically free from a system that you're unable to free yourself from psychologically, in utter disregard of your current physical relationship to it.

The best description of self-liberation I know of is Frederick Douglass’ account of his fist-and-foot fight with “Mr. Covey”, his slave master at the time, which neither of them “won”.

But when you read it (2-3 minutes’ worth), you’ll have no doubt who won, hands down.

Here’s the upshot:

This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom, and revived within me a sense of my own manhood. It recalled the departed self-confidence, and inspired me again with ‘a determination to be free. The gratification afforded by the triumph was a full compensation for whatever else might follow, even death itself.. He only can understand the deep satisfaction which I experienced, who has himself repelled by force the bloody arm of slavery. I felt as I never felt before. It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom. My long-crushed spirit rose, cowardice departed, bold defiance took its place; and I now resolved that, however long I might remain a slave in form, the day had passed forever when I could be a slave in fact. I did not hesitate to let it be known of me, that the white man who expected to succeed in whipping, must also succeed in killing me.

From this time I was never again what might be called fairly whipped, though I remained a slave four years afterwards. I had several fights, but was never whipped.

The account of the fight itself is well worth the reading time. The story is even more striking in light of what he wrote just ten pages before on page 63:

If at any one time of my life more than another, I was made to drink the bitterest dregs of slavery, that time was during the first six months of my stay with Mr. Covey. We were worked in all weathers. It was never too hot or too cold; it could never rain, blow, hail, or snow, too hard for us to work in the field. Work, work, work, was scarcely more the order of the day than of the night. The longest days were too short for him, and the shortest nights too long for him, I was somewhat unmanageable when | first went there, but a few months of this discipline tamed me. Mr. Covey succeeded in breaking me. I was broken in body, soul, and spirit. My natural elasticity was crushed, my intellect languished, the disposition to read departed, the cheerful spark that lingered about my eye died; the dark night of slavery closed in upon me ; and behold a man transformed into a brute!

From shadow of a human being to unbowed, undauntable, and undefeated for the rest of his remaining 4 years “a slave in form”.

It wasn’t magic. It’s just what happens when you realize you’re past putting up with the shit anymore.

https://archive.org/details/douglasfred00dougrich/page/72/mode/2up?q=covey

entries.html:
Perceived limitations, whether they originate in honest, careful thinking or paranoid terror, cannot be true. The question whether they are true is ridiculous as long as we refuse to move out of the hypothetical and into the factual because, by definition, the hypothetical only has a place in the absence of fact.

What’s more, there is only one way to obtain facts: doing something. Honestly exposing ourselves to and interacting with what’s really going on.

That means precisely: moving out of the hypothetical and into the actual. We have no facts other than from experience.

This is obvious and easily demonstrable. As soon we allow facts into our mental mix, hypotheticals such as the occult, beliefs, superstitions, delusions, etc., automatically lose their power. You can see this happen with a person in real time. It’s unmistakable. You can watch their mind shift into a completely different, far saner and calmer mode. It’s not hard at all to induce this, except for one thing:

To the degree that a person clings to their infantilism, they will fight against accepting certain facts into their mental mix, even if only to admit them as considerable, let alone consider them honestly.

The reason for this has nothing at all to do with what’s “really real” or factual or intelligent or advisable. It concerns just one, simple, far more basic thing: they feel, however consciously or not, the mortal threat waiting to accost them were they to merely admit: not that certain information is factual, but only that it could be factual. The door to investigating that angle must remain blocked by pretending there’s nothing to investigate. The results of investigating are not the imminent danger. The openness and honesty involved in real investigation are the killers of their blind fidelity to the narrative they’re clinging to for sanity and dear life: the narrative for which, undoubtedly, they have already sacrificed much in order to stay clung.

It’s no wonder that all the most important areas of human life—personal relationships, business, government, and especially those infernal bedfellows religion and the military—revolve around the core of “sacrifice” and are permeated with its theme.

Such people are gruesomely enslaved. We call them “cultists” when they seem wildly strange and different from ourselves, pretending that our own particular enslavement to our own particular survival/salvation narratives is virtuous, while theirs is vile.

There’s a simple, foolproof litmus test for cultism. It tells us where a person’s rationality ends and their cultism begins—including our own:

Mark the point at which a person refuses to look at a possibility for fear that it might turn out to be a fact.

Herbert Spencer’s statement, unwittingly no doubt, captured the hallmark trait of all cultists: zealous disparagement of unwanted information and those who bring it to them for fear of the mere possibility that it might prove to be true.

entries.name: Millard J Melnyk
entries.html:
I was recently asked, “Given that the authorities keep lying to the people, why do the people keep believing the authorities?”

Well, because when you boil authoritarianism down to its essence and basic structure, it’s incontrovertible: we were all mind-fucked into thinking like cultists.

The foremost aspect of cultism is infantilism. Think about it. To believe authorities requires suspending our own better judgment and knowledge in order to adopt the position of a child before them.

Infantilism guarantees codependence.

Codependence guarantees cultism.

That’s what religious training and “education” are primarily about (and always have been), and that’s why they take so long. University, too. It takes a lotta-lotta work to break down our natural self-confidence and abuse us into relying interminably on others instead of maturing and becoming competent in our own right.

Sure, they taught us stuff, for good or ill—but before they taught us anything worth knowing, and far and away more than they informed us or made us smarter, they conditioned us by both the method of teaching itself (Freire’s “banking model of education” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking_model_of_education, by systemic Pavlovian conditioning (seats all in a row that we might as well have been strapped to, bells to signal “passing periods” and mark “tardies”, regimentation throughout, etc.), and above all by authoritarian punishment and reward.

None of that aimed at bettering us in ways that we would agree are better, but rather to better make us venerate and serve our higher-ups.

That was the first 15–20 years of our lives, thanks to virtually every authority in our lives, and it gets reinforced incessantly ever afterwards, known as “socialization”. And anyone who resists the conditioning or rebels against it gets stigmatized as “antisocial”, having a “problem with authority”.

The problem isn’t with people who insist on being independent and free—it’s with everyone else who insists that we must all behave like children and submit/defer to and obey our “leaders”.

For my part: fuck that. They’re not my “leaders”. The only leaders I have are people I choose to follow if and when they demonstrate they’re worth following for a while, until I’ve learned what I needed from them. Anyone who’s worth following will be more than happy when a follower stops following, because they’re competent, so they have no need for followers.

Isn’t that what good parents hope: that their children will leave them, become independent, and eventually surpass them? False leaders (they used to be called “false prophets”) have no intention of being left or surpassed. They require interminable codependence, which means interminable infantilism.

How many authorities have you known who demonstrated their follow-worthy competence before they demanded that you follow them? I’m talking about parents, too. How many so-called “leaders” who presumed authority over us made sure that the choice to follow them was always squarely ours?

We’ve sunk so low that the response I usually get to that is, “But, how could that work? That would end up being a disaster!”

I just shake my head. Among fools, ignorance is taken as the limit of possibility.

Compare how many real leaders you’ve seen to how many would-be authorities demanded obedience from you—not only before demonstrating any competence that would support their demand, but far more often despite grave, repeated, demonstrated incompetence?

Elected leaders, those that they appoint to positions of power, and those that they hire into positions of authority never demonstrate their competence to us. At best, they give us promises, and their success rates in keeping those promises rarely rise above the single-digits.

No wonder, because this is what authority is for in the first place: it enables the incompetent to demand what only the competent should ever dare demand, completely bypassing every question of competence.

But the competent don’t do that, do they? Think of all the seriously competent people you’ve known. How many of them demanded that you obey them, even if just in their areas of competence? How many demanded that you obey them merely because they occupied a position that legitimized their demand wholly apart from any and all question of competence?

Competent people don’t need to demand obedience, because their power lies in being very good at doing things—not this fakery they call “power” which is nothing more than an ability to get others to do for them what they cannot do for themselves.

Authority is what fools and idiots need in order to control the competence of others, because they’ve got no confidence whatsoever in their ability to do it themselves.

Just witness how difficult and expensive it is to keep their massive webs of lies intact and how easy it is, despite all their efforts, to undermine, subvert, and overthrow them, their so-called "narratives".

That's why it's always been true that if they're pushed too far, defied too badly, exposed too much—or far more often, long before a credible threat materializes, when they get terrified shitless at the mere hint that they might be pushed and defied and exposed—they always resort to the same MO: since they can't touch our souls, they threaten and mutilate and kill our bodies.

So, just like scorpions cannot but do according to their nature, toadies—for fear of harm, pain, injury, and death—all give their souls over to carry scorpions on their backs across the pond, then are astonished by the inevitable deadly sting.

Such have we all been, to one degree or another—most often lock, stock, and barrel.

But the problem isn't our natures. The problem is that we lie about our natures. The only reason we're stuck in an apparently endless, vicious cycle is that we lie about it—which is the single key factor perpetuating the cycle.

Without our lies, we could not pretend that it's necessary and unavoidable to let scorpions climb aboard our backs. What's more, we could swim across the pond and leave them stranded.

It's so easy to see who has sold their souls: everyone who refuses to take the path to freedom under the bullshit excuse that it can't be taken.

Ignorance and incredulity are in no way tantamount to impossibility. Pretending them to be so is just further proof of toadiness.

Toady bullshit is not real and it is not true—the exact same bullshit that every one of us who has started off on that “impossible” path has proven with just our single, first step to be a putrid, malicious lie .

Take taxes. Everyone who pays taxes has funded the genocidal rampage that has been the American Way since the inception of the country—first, on a national stage and, since WW2, on the global stage.

Which indigenous peoples has the US failed to decimate or completely wipe out? Which indigenous culture did it not attack, outlaw, and completely stigmatize or even erase in most cases?
